item.title: Delicacy offers relief from Sichuan's fiery spices
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
In the back corner of a kitchen in Meishan, Sichuan province, beside a stove hissing with chili oil and popping peppercorns, sits a jar that never makes it onto the menu. Its contents — a colorful mix of greens, reds, yellows and whites — rest submerged in an opaque brine. The world knows Sichuan for kung pao chicken, mapo tofu, its mouth-numbing hotpot and the mellow depth of doubanjiang (fermented bean paste), but ask any local what binds those bold flavors together, and the answer is likely paocai — pickled vegetables. It also elevates Sichuan breakfast staples such as noodles, steamed buns and congee, imparting a signature tang to classic dishes such as fish-flavored shredded pork, sour vegetable fish and sour-radish duck soup. "Sichuan paocai is crisp and not overly salty," said 56-year-old chef Jiang Ming. "The lactic fermentation yields a natural, earthy sourness that vinegar lacks, making it an ideal flavor enhancer." In Meishan, this tradition has been elevated to an almost architectural scale. At a workshop in the China Paocai City industrial park, nearly 5,000 giant clay jars stand in neat rows, each about 1.6 meters tall. He Yanping, 49, a provincial-level inheritor of Dongpo paocai-making techniques, presses his ear to a lid as a gentle gurgle escapes from within. "That's the sound of lactic acid bacteria fermenting and releasing gas," he said. The craft takes its name from Su Dongpo — the celebrated Song Dynasty (960-1279) poet and gourmand who was born in Meishan. The legacy of Su, a passionate maker himself, lent the pickle its enduring cultural identity. The roots of Chinese pickled vegetables stretch back even further, over 3,000 years in fact, to the pre-Qin period (before 221 BC), when early references to zu, or pickled vegetables, appear in classics such as the Book of Songs and the Rites of Zhou. This deep historical lineage found its way into local customs. By the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), a jar of paocai had become an essential part of a bride's dowry — a portable legacy of flavor carried into married life. Traditional Dongpo paocai is made in a large earthenware jar. Fresh vegetables are packed inside and fully submerged in the "mother brine", or laomu shui — a living culture passed down through generations. The lid is sealed with a water lock, allowing gases to escape while keeping oxygen out. What follows is daily care and patient waiting. "The secret lies in the mother brine, teeming with the specific strains of lactic acid bacteria that give Dongpo paocai its distinctive flavor," He said. To outsiders, pickled vegetables may call to mind kimchi or sauerkraut, but Sichuan paocai is different. Radishes, carrots, cabbage, long beans, young ginger, red Sichuan chili peppers and bamboo shoots are packed whole or in chunks into a seasoned brine of water, salt, Sichuan peppercorns and other spices, often with a bit of baijiu. Within hours or a day or two at most, they emerge with a clean, crisp sourness and a subtle fragrance. "This water-based fermentation method sets Dongpo paocai apart from most other pickling methods in China or abroad," He said. "The credit goes to the Sichuan Basin's mild climate — free from freezing winters and scorching summers — which keeps the lactic acid bacteria active year-round." Another defining feature is the brief fermentation period — sometimes just hours — which yields a lower-salt product with a distinctly crisp texture. What began as a local craft is evolving into a global curiosity, with a growing number of foreign visitors flocking to the China Paocai City industrial park to master the craft. Among them is Hajar Wassila, a Moroccan student who joined a DIY session at the workshop of Sichuan Laotanzi Food Co. Guided by instructors, she packed her jar with vegetables, garlic, red Sichuan chili peppers and carrots, pressing them firmly beneath the brine. "When I smell it, I want to taste it immediately," she said, holding up the jar with a grin. "I love pickles and tried to make them before, but failed. Now I've finally got the secret." At the Sichuan Dongpo Chinese Paocai Industrial Technology Research Institute, more than 11,000 microbial strains are preserved, supporting local enterprises in developing new products and refining quality, according to Wang Dongdong, deputy director of the institute. "By screening superior strains and developing advanced production technologies, we have reduced salt content, enhanced flavor and accelerated fermentation, while ensuring consistently stable quality," Wang said. "We are also researching the use of specific strains to develop pickles with the potential to help lower blood sugar and lipid levels," he added.

item.title: 300 strangers attend Uygur wedding after viral post
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
300 strangers attend Uygur wedding after viral post Earlier this month, a Uygur wedding in Yarkant county of Kashgar prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, became an unexpected nationwide celebration. More than 300 strangers traveled from across the country to share in the joy and blessings of the occasion. The scene that followed, brimming with music and dance, cheer and laughter, was later captured in online posts and videos that spread the festive vibes even farther and wider. The story began when the groom's mother Zoram Seyit posted a digital invitation on the short-video sharing platform Douyin on Aug 3, expecting only family and friends to respond. But when a curious user from Central China's Henan province asked if they could attend and the host family replied with a simple "yes", the post went viral overnight. On Aug 8, the wedding day, the banquet hall was filled with guests from diverse regions and ethnic backgrounds, all gathered for the same celebration. Men and women, many in their finest attire, sang and danced throughout the day. Groom Akramjan Omar said his online guests joined in every part of the celebration, from the midday procession to escort the bride to the wedding hall and the main ceremony in the afternoon, to the after-party that stretched past 9 pm. He had been unaware of his mother's post until the next morning, when he woke up to find it had already racked up over 10,000 likes. For a family that has run a Xinjiang cuisine restaurant in Henan for nearly three decades, more guests meant more joy. However, as the numbers kept climbing — likes, comments and promises to attend — the initial excitement gave way to a practical concern: how to take good care of these guests, especially when they had no way of knowing how many would actually show up. The family then trimmed their original guest list from 500 relatives and friends on each of the bride's and groom's sides to 200 per side and reserved the second floor, which offered a full view of the hall, for strangers traveling from afar. Food supplies were doubled, featuring local specialties such as pilaf, baked stuffed buns, seasonal and dried fruits, as well as wedding sweets, while a Mandarin-speaking partner was added alongside the Uygur-language master of ceremonies. Many guests attempted to hand over their cash gifts, following Chinese wedding customs, but the host family declined most of them. Akramjan Omar said he was touched at one point seeing people who clearly didn't really know how to dance moving anyway, their faces lit up with pure enjoyment. At the end of the night, the newlyweds and their unexpected guests gathered for a group photo. Warm hospitality Wei Lixi, 20, from South China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, was on a solo road trip in Kashgar city when he saw the invitation on Douyin. He had his vehicle washed for the occasion and joined the groom's procession early that morning. The groom led everyone in a dance, and guests were handed party poppers to set off during the liveliest moments. At first, Wei worried about intruding — but the hosts welcomed the out-of-town visitors with open arms. "The air was electric. I felt like part of one big family," he said. Hao Shuhui, 24, from Henan, married into a Xinjiang family earlier this year. She dug through her wardrobe for a bright red dress and made her way to the Uygur family that has longstanding ties with her hometown. The hosts were warm enough to ease her shyness. A groomsman had set up a WeChat group in advance, sharing a few do's and don'ts and encouraging the guests to speak up about any needs. The netizens, meanwhile, were worried about causing trouble. A guest in his 30s surnamed Tang from Shandong province said, "It was incredibly infectious, even for those of us Han people who aren't particularly good at singing or dancing." He added that he had immersed himself in the warmth, hospitality and optimism of the Uygur friends, and felt a genuine bond between people of different ethnic backgrounds. Guests like him, too, began chatting and sharing stories of their travels and lives. Emerging tourism draw Grand and lively Uygur weddings have long attracted visitors and sparked fascination across China. In May 2025, the variety show HAHAHAHAHA re-created a ceremony through role-play. On Aug 12, the Uygur wedding of celebrity couple Madina Memet and Jiang Chao sparked heated online discussions. Some Douyin posts generated several hundred thousand likes, with the most popular exceeding 2 million. A typical Uygur wedding unfolds with a morning session hosted by the bride's family, followed by the bride-pickup and a transitional segment for the younger crowd that features dancing, the bouquet toss and photo sessions, as well as a banquet by the groom's side with a formal veil-lifting ceremony. Singing and dancing accompany every stage of the wedding. Days before, a "consultation tea party" allows both families to get acquainted and exchange betrothal gifts, while days after, close family members and friends will gather at the bride's home for a visit. The invitation post for the Yarkant wedding has to date accumulated more than 10 million views and some 77,000 comments. Some netizens posted their own wedding invitations on Douyin, while others simply asked: "Can I come?" Experiencing a Uygur wedding has gradually become a tourism draw in Xinjiang. Some banquet venues in Urumqi and Kashgar offer viewing areas on the second-floor mezzanines for tourists to watch real ceremonies live. In Kashgar city, 26-year-old visitor Zhang Yao observed a wedding this way. "The women wore an abundance of ornate jewelry. Their dresses had a bold, vivid theme color but were different in design, all absolutely stunning," she said, while also noting the importance of respecting the hosts on their big day. Yao Jiahui tried her luck on Thursday and happened upon a wedding. A bridesmaid took her along on the dance floor. Aunties asked her in Uygur if she was enjoying the event. "It's all in the dance," she said. Han Yawei and Hu Dongyue contributed to this story. Contact the writers at fangaiqing@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Motor event offers key market outlook
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Motor event offers key market outlook Chengdu show features technology, overseas growth and competition Around 120 major domestic and international automakers are showcasing about 1,600 vehicles at the Chengdu Motor Show, highlighting the latest developments in electrification and intelligent technologies. The 10-day event, which kicked off on Friday, is the first major A-level auto show in China in the second half of the year and an important indicator of the market outlook for the months ahead. "A wide range of debut models across different segments is displayed, giving visitors and consumers a clear picture of the latest industry developments and market trends," said Liu Guoliang, general manager of Hannover Milano Fairs Shanghai, one of the event's organizers. The show comes as China's auto market undergoes a profound structural shift. Passenger vehicle sales fell 24.3 percent year-on-year to 8.29 million units in the first half of 2026. While sales of traditional fuel-powered passenger vehicles dropped 31.9 percent year-on-year to 3.69 million units, new energy vehicle sales rose 7.3 percent during the same period, with their market share continuing to expand. "China's auto market is experiencing an interplay of ice and fire," Liu said, referring to the contraction of the overall market and the accelerating development of electrified smart vehicles. The changing market is also pushing automakers to compete less on price and more on technology, product value and brand differentiation. The Chengdu show provides a snapshot of the growing technological strength of Chinese automakers. BYD has brought together its Dynasty and Ocean series as well as Denza, Fangchengbao and Yangwang, showcasing fast-charging and advanced driver-assistance technologies. Chery Group is displaying 38 models from all five of its brands, while Great Wall Motor, Geely Galaxy, Hongqi, BAIC, Deepal, Voyah and other Chinese brands are expanding their new energy and intelligent vehicle portfolios. Wang Xia, president of the automotive sub-council at the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, said the industry's competitiveness should not be judged solely by short-term sales. "Sales are a fast variable," Wang said, while technology, brands, partnerships and industrial ecosystems are "slow variables" that more fundamentally determine competitiveness. China accounted for 35.6 percent of global automobile patent publications over the past decade, according to figures cited by Wang. Chinese companies also occupied 17 positions on the 2026 global top 100 automotive suppliers list. "China used to exchange its market for technology; today, China is using technology to compete in the world," Wang said. The transformation is increasingly visible overseas. China exported 5.1 million vehicles in the first half of 2026, up 65.3 percent year-on-year, while new energy vehicle exports more than doubled to 2.36 million units, according to figures cited at the event. Chinese automakers are also moving from exporting vehicles toward building overseas production facilities and integrating into local supply chains. More than 100 Chinese vehicle production bases have been established overseas, with overseas production capacity exceeding 2.5 million vehicles, Wang said. At the same time, joint ventures are taking on new forms, with multinational automakers increasingly relying on Chinese technologies and R&D capabilities and exploring ways to export products developed in China to global markets. At the Chengdu show, for example, Dongfeng Peugeot and Dongfeng Citroen are highlighting their transition toward intelligent electrification. BMW has started taking orders for its long-wheelbase Neue Klasse iX3. Other major brands including Audi, Volkswagen, Buick, Toyota and Honda are displaying their new electric and intelligent models tailored for Chinese customers. The event's organizers also integrated a wider range of immersive experiences this year. For example, a dedicated model-car zone has been set up for the first time, alongside limited-time weekend special events. "Our vision is to build the show into an automotive-culture carnival open to all members of the public," Liu said. The importance of the Chengdu show extends beyond the exhibition halls. Chengdu, capital of Sichuan province, has developed into a major automotive manufacturing and consumption center in western China, supported by an increasingly complete new energy and intelligent connected vehicle industrial chain. A dedicated exhibition area for the "Chengdu-made" intelligent connected vehicle industry chain has been established for the first time, showcasing technologies in batteries, electric drive systems and intelligent connectivity. Vehicles produced in Chengdu by brands including Volvo, Zeekr, Lynk& Co and Jetta are also on display. The show is also connecting local manufacturers with overseas buyers, reflecting Chengdu's growing role as a gateway for Chinese vehicles entering global markets. For the Chinese auto industry, this year's Chengdu show is more than a platform for new-car launches, analysts said. It is also a test of how automakers can respond to a shrinking market, increasingly demanding consumers and intensifying global competition, they said. The message emerging from the event is clear: China's auto industry is moving into a new phase in which technological capability, global competitiveness and value creation are becoming increasingly important alongside sales volume.

item.title: China renews alerts for rainstorms, typhoon
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
China renews alerts for rainstorms, typhoon BEIJING - China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) on Monday renewed a yellow alert for rainstorms and a blue alert for the 19th typhoon of this year, with heavy rainfall and strong winds forecast to affect multiple regions of the country. From 8 am Monday to 8 am Tuesday, torrential rain is expected to lash parts of Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Taiwan, Hainan, Jiangxi, Hunan, Hubei, Yunnan, Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang, according to the NMC. Intense downpours will hit southeastern Zhejiang, the eastern coastal areas of Fujian, northern Guangdong, most parts of Taiwan Island, and eastern Liaoning, with some areas in Taiwan likely to see exceptionally heavy rain of 250 to 300 millimeters. The affected areas will experience short-term heavy rainfall, with hourly precipitation reaching 20 to 50 millimeters, accompanied by thunderstorms and gales, the NMC said. Meanwhile, the 19th typhoon of this year was located at 5 am Monday in the Beibu Gulf, about 185 kilometers southwest of Beihai city in South China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, with maximum winds of 23 meters per second near its center. It is expected to track eastward from Monday night and then travel northward at a speed of 5 to 10 kilometers per hour, gradually approaching the coastal areas from Guangxi to the western Leizhou Peninsula in Guangdong province. The NMC has advised local governments to take precautionary measures. China has a four-tier color-coded weather warning system, with red representing the most severe, followed by orange, yellow and blue.

item.title: AI amping up gaming developers
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
AI amping up gaming developers Rapid development of technology fundamentally restructuring process The effective application of artificial intelligence technologies and further global business expansion are seen as the key drivers shaping the future of China's gaming industry, business leaders and developers said at the 23rd China Digital Entertainment Expo and Conference (ChinaJoy), which took place from July 31 to Aug 3 in Shanghai. The rapid development of AI technologies — such as large language models, multimodal models and AI agents — is fundamentally restructuring the entire game development and operations process. Targeting specifically the gaming industry, the AI gaming cloud has been booming over the past few years. According to a recent research report by United States-based market consultancy IDC, the AI gaming cloud basically refers to the AI technologies, products and services used by game developers throughout the production process, from game design and prototyping to game development and testing, as well as game publishing and operations. The report showed that China's AI gaming cloud market reached 1.86 billion yuan ($275 million) last year. The sector is expected to maintain a compound annual growth rate of about 91.6 percent over the next five years, hitting 11 billion yuan by 2029 and contributing more than half of the overall gaming cloud market. Baidu AI Cloud, one of the earliest Chinese tech giants engaging in the sector, took about 51 percent of the nation's AI gaming cloud market share, said the report. To date, it has established in-depth partnerships with more than half of the nation's leading game companies and over 100 innovative AI gaming firms, providing full-stack AI capabilities to companies such as miHoYo, Net-Ease Games, 37 Interactive Entertainment and Unity China. Among Baidu AI Cloud's offerings, its AI Heterogeneous Compute serves as the AI infrastructure that allows game developers to focus on essential content creation without worrying about computing power management. Baidu Qianfan, an enterprise-grade, all-in-one large model platform, is built around agents, providing the gaming industry with a one-stop platform for model access, agent development and data intelligence services. It can support end-to-end AI collaboration across the entire workflow from text creation and character design to 3D modeling, animation production and code development, helping game developers improve both creative efficiency and quality. "What AI truly unlocks is not just the content production capacity, but the gaming industry's ability to continuously create new gameplay, new characters and new experiences," said Zhang Wei, vice-president of Baidu Intelligent Cloud. Baidu's AI solutions have empowered gaming businesses, such as SingularDance and SEELE AI. SingularDance is an innovative tech firm focused on the development of AI emotional companionship and hyper-personified intelligent agents. Edward Lu Hongyi, founder and CEO of SingularDance, highlighted that they are committed to creating virtual characters that not only know how to chat with users, but also possess distinct, stable, independent and continuously evolving personalities with a "soul". With a core focus on restructuring traditional game development workflows, SEELE AI is a tech firm focused on AI-native games and interactive worlds powered by foundational models. Collaborating with Baidu, it enables users to automatically generate interactive 3D game worlds via natural language using multimodal inputs, such as text and images, to complete the entire workflow, including character modeling, animation generation, scene construction, game mechanics and narrative presentation. "We aim to enable every creative individual to collaborate with AI agents via natural language, quickly transforming their ideas into game worlds that are accessible, playable, editable and continuously iterable. So every gamer can actually become a game developer, and generate income from their creation," said Liu Bo, the company's partner of business operations. Hu Xin, assistant to the chairman of Zhejiang Century Huatong Group, said that currently, AI has been fully integrated into more than 80 percent of the company's entire workflow of game development, which is also the case for most businesses in the gaming industry. The future competition within the industry would be much about "creativity, aesthetics and user insights". The group, which is the parent company of Shengqu Games and Century Games, is also actively ramping up efforts in globalization and international collaboration for sustained growth. Following a fruitful 17-year partnership with South Korea's NC Corp, Shengqu Games unveiled the two sides' new collaboration on the much anticipated game AION 2 on July 30 during the ChinaJoy 2026 expo.

item.title: Mapping ground reality
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Mapping ground reality Substrate survey team digs deep across 83 key black soil counties to unearth secrets of the earth and learn how to improve farming It takes nature about 200 to 400 years to build about 1 centimeter of black soil, a key element in China's food security. In many parts of Northeast China, that soil is thinning. But the key to saving it, a geologist argues, lies not only in the soil itself, but also in the ground beneath it. A ground substrate survey team from the Langfang Natural Resources Comprehensive Survey Center of the China Geological Survey has completed a survey across 83 key black soil counties on more than 410,000 square kilometers of land. Their job was not to look at the soil, but to drill through it, down to dozens of meters, to see what lies underneath. "On the surface, the black soil looks uniform. Drill into it, and the profile changes completely," said Chen Peng, a member of the center's ground substrate survey team. Some fields sit on a thick layer of clay. Water and nutrients stay put. Others sit on sand and gravel. Water and fertilizer drain straight through. In some places, bedrock is just below the black soil. And once the top layer thins, recovery is painfully slow, he added. "Underneath, one field can be completely different from another. We cannot protect them in the same way," the 44-year-old said.

item.title: A Shanghai slingshot for overseas expansion
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
A Shanghai slingshot for overseas expansion Government services help clear obstacles for companies entering foreign markets Going global — a pressing goal of many Chinese companies — is not only about grasping the big picture. Nuanced details, such as what can be demonstrated in a product commercial, for example, may jeopardize a company's future prospects in an unfamiliar new market. With eight years' experience in overseas markets, Shanghai-based gaming company Boke Technology learned this lesson, said the company's general counsel Wang Sijia. One product commercial for a Southeast Asian market featured exaggerated creative content. It depicted a hamburger that had accidentally fallen on the ground being stepped on, which may have been construed as disrespectful due to cultural sensitivities. Wang said sometimes it's difficult for companies to make such fine distinctions. However, this is one of the smaller challenges Chinese companies may be confronted with when they enter a new market. Abiding by local market entry regulations and contract formats are even larger issues, she said. "The biggest headache about going global is the information gap. Companies do not know who to turn to or what they can do when a problem occurs," she said. When publishing companies enter a new market, for example, they often have to work with local service providers for the first time. Without access to reliable information or experience in collaboration, it is extremely difficult to find the right partners. A company's own internal risk management capabilities are usually insufficient, Wang added. "The cost of trial and error can be prohibitively high," she said.

item.title: 'Sprouting' partnerships
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
'Sprouting' partnerships Forum highlights growing business collaborations between Beijing, Moscow The 2026 Russia-China Business Forum titled "Sprouts: Russia and China — Mutually Beneficial Cooperation" opened on Aug 16 in Kazan, the capital of the Republic of Tatarstan, bringing together over 50 business sessions, eight Chinese provincial delegations, and numerous Russian federal officials. More than 10,000 square meters of exhibition space showcased cooperation in logistics, finance, healthcare, industry, agriculture, creative economy, and artificial intelligence. Against this backdrop of expanding ties, Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui delivered an address at the forum highlighting the latest trade figures. "Sino-Russian trade and economic cooperation is demonstrating steady growth. From January to July 2026, the volume of bilateral trade reached $159 billion, which represents a 26 percent increase compared to the same period last year. It is quite possible that a new all-time high will be set by the end of the year," Zhang said. Local currency settlements also took center stage. Zhou Liqun, chairman of the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce in Russia, voiced strong support for bilateral settlements in national currencies during an interview of the forum.

item.title: Every small effort matters for China-US friendship
item.description:

Every small effort matters for China-US friendship Share - WeChat
Twenty-seven years later, American Ronald Sakolsky returned to Ordos, China's Inner Mongolia, to reunite with Yin Yuzhen, who transformed his donation into a vast forest. Sharing memories over fresh fruit, Sakolsky said that China-US friendship needs more people to take action. "Even a small amount can become a forest," he added.
